newsitem.title: USA: Freeze damage to Kansas HRW wheat believed minor.
newsitem.headline: Freeze damage to Kansas HRW wheat believed minor.

text.p: U.S. hard red winter wheat in Kansas may have sustained minor damage following freezing temperatures overnight, but the most vulnerable crops in the south of the state probably escaped unscathed, a leading agronomist said.

"The southern third of the state dodged a bullet. Another three to five degrees and we probably could have seen some damage in that area," said Jim Shroyer, extension wheat agronomist at Kansas State University.
Shroyer said there may have been minor tiller loss around the coldest spots, Goodland and Tribune in western Kansas.
He noted that wheat had jointed in southern Kansas and could therefore be damaged if temperatures dropped to the upper teens or low 20s Fahrenheit for an extended period.
Further north in the state, wheat had not jointed and so would only be threatened by temperatures in the low teens F for an extended period, Shroyer said.
Lows early Monday dropped to 14 degrees in Goodland, in north-west Kansas, but temperatures were warmer further south, according to Weather Services Corp.
"It was very cold but probably not quite cold enough to damage the crop," said WSC meteorologist Joel Burgio.
Shroyer warned, however, that it was possible that actual temperatures in the fields were lower than the official readings and therefore damage may be greater than currently believed.
"It is usually colder out in farmer fields than the official temperatures on the edge of town," he noted.
Shroyer said dry conditions in western Kansas may also increase the potential threat to the crop.
"Wet soil will keep the temperatures a little warmer," he said, noting wheat in northern Kansas is within 10 days of jointing.

Further north in Nebraska, another leading hard red winter wheat producing state, the major threat to the crop came from strong winds rather than cold temperatures, according to Nebraska University professor Stephen Baenziger.

"Obviously the wind is tough but it is not unusual. I don't expect signficiant losses in any part of the state and certainly not due to the cold. It would be only due to the wind. If a wheat crop can't take that kind of cold it doesn't deserve to be grown in this state," he said.
Nebraska was the fourth largest US HRW wheat producing state last year, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. Kansas was the leading US HRW wheat state.
Oklahoma and Texas, the second and third largest HRW wheat states respectively, are located further south and did not experience threatening temperatures.
